div.head: Ine 19
div.ab: LXIII. Cyninges geneat, gif his wer bið twelfhund scill., he mot swerian for syxtig hida, gif he bið huslgengea.
LXIII. Cyninges geneat, gif his wer biþ twelfhun: scill', he mot swerigen for sixtig hida, g.. he bið huslgenga.
LXIII. Cyninges geneat, gif his wer bið CXX scll', he mot swerigan for LX hida, gif he bið huslgenga.
Be cinges geneate. Cyninges geneat, gyf his wer bið twelfhund scill', he mot swerian for sixti hída, gyf he bið huslgenga.

Regis geneat (id est uillanus [colonus fiscalinus]) si wera eius sit twelfhund scill. (id est duodecies C sol.), potest iurare pro LX hidis (id est pro sex hominibus), si sit hulsgenga (id est duodecimhindus uel ħusbonda).
[Be cinges geneate.] Cyninges geneat gif his wer bið twelfhund scill., he mot swerian for syxtig hida, gif he bið huslgengea.
{LXIII} Cyninges geneat, gif his wer bið twelfhund sciƚƚ, he mot swerian for syxtig hida, gif he bið huslgenga.
Ein Königs-Gefolgsmann, wenn sein Wergeld 1200 Schill. beträgt, der darf schwören für 60 Hiden, vorausgesetzt, er sei Abendmahlsgänger.
A king’s retainer, if his wergeld amounts to 1200 shillings, may swear for 60 hides, provided he is a communicant.
A member of the king's household, if his wergeld is 1200 shillings, shall be allowed to swear for 60 hides, if he is a communicant.
A king’s geneat, if his wergild is 1200 shillings, may, if he is a communicant, swear for 60 hides.
A member of the king’s household, if his wer is 1,200 shillings, may swear [an oath in the value of] sixty hides, if he is a communicant.

‘Bauer (s. d. Gl 1e) auf fremdem Lande, Gutsinsasse’ (wie Ine 22) missversteht Q, gemäss der einzigen Bed., die das Wort im 12. Jh. behielt, und umschreibt es durch einen Normann. und (in spät. Rez.) einen Fränk. Rechtsausdruck. Glossare geben als Synonyma tungebur, inbuend, oðres eardes landsæta. Ine aber meint Gefolgsadel; s. d. Gl 2h. Aus dem ‘wenn’ folgt vielleicht, dass nicht jeder (wie später der Königsthegn) 1200 Schilling Wergeld (s. d. Gl 4ff.) hatte. Obwohl Price geltend macht, mancher Thegn im Domesday trage niedere Dienstlast, so beweist dies nicht für Q, dass je Gefolgsadel und Fronbauer gleichstanden

Q misunderstands it as ‘peasant (see that word in Gl 1e) on another’s land, inhabitant of an estate’ (as in Ine 22), in accordance with the only meaning the word retained in the 12th cent., and paraphrases it with a Norman and (in a later recension) a Frankish legal term. Glossaries give as synonyms tungebur, inbuend, oðres eardes landsæta. Ine, however, means the nobility of the retinue; see that word in Gl 2h. From the ‘if’ it perhaps follows that not every one of them (as later every king’s thegn) had a wergild (see that word in Gl 4ff.) of 1200 shillings. Although Price points out that many a thegn in Domesday bears a low burden of service, this does not prove, in support of Q, that the nobility of the retinue and peasants owing labour-service were ever on an equal footing

note.seg: huslgenga. H, B, Bu.

It would seem that the number of hides for which a ‘twelvehynde’ man was entitled by his birth to swear was thirty at this time. In that case, the value of the oath is doubled if he is a member of the king’s household, and is at the same time a communicant (see Chadwick, Anglo-Saxon Institutions, p. 136 f.). According to Liebermann all twelfhynde men were assumed to be communicants (see Liebermann, Die Eideshufen bei den Angelsachsen).
The expression Cyninges geneat occurs in the Sax. Chron. ann. 897, where the death in battle is recorded of Æðelferð cynges geneat—a fact which would seem to indicate that these men were persons of some position (see Chadwick, Anglo-Saxon Institutions, p. 137).

note.label: geneat
note.seg: This word denotes originally “a member of a household” and may in these early laws be being used quite generally. By the eleventh century it is used of men who hold land from a lord and pay rent and certain honourable services (especially riding duties), and who seem to correspond to a class called “radcnihts” in Domesday Book. In its technical sense a geneat differs from a gesith in not normally being of the noble class. On gesith, see p. 396, n. 4. 1
